songs.name: Goin' Down The Road Feeling Bad

supporting_acts: New Riders of the Purple Sage

ai_show_review.summary: High‑energy Lovelight showcase with tight jams and stellar drums
ai_show_review.blurb: Pigpen’s organ‑driven Turn On Your Lovelight dominates the set, backed by a crisp Sunshine Daydream vibe. Jerry shines on early leads like Cumberland Blues while the dual‑drum duet adds an electrifying pulse. Strong renditions of Hard To Handle and Good Lovin’ round out an inspiring early‑71 performance.
ai_show_review.review: The Seattle Center Arena show on January 24, 1971 finds the Dead riding a wave of high‑octane energy from the first note. Pigpen’s organ magic is front‑and‑center as the band rolls through two consecutive Turn On Your Lovelight stretches, each segue into Not Fade Away and Goin’ Down The Road Feeling Bad feeling seamless despite a curfew break that pushed the music into the early morning hours. Jerry Garcia delivers his trademark soaring lead on Cumberland Blues and keeps the tone bright throughout, though later moments drift a bit sloppy. Phil “bombs” with a powerful bass foundation, especially during the transition into Uncle John’s Band‑style jams, while Bob Weir locks in solid rhythm guitar and vocal harmonies despite a few high‑pitched early vocals. The drum department shines: Bill Kreutzmann’s foot‑pedal work culminates in a standout solo, and Mickey Hart’s cowbell adds his signature sparkle, creating one of the rare, exhilarating dual‑drum duets of this era. Overall, the soundboard capture is good—clear enough to hear the crisp organ on Sunshine Daydream and the clean guitar tones—making this a must‑listen for fans of early‑70s Dead energy.

best_recording.reason: Decent soundboard tape with clear organ and guitar, crisp Sunshine Daydream, and only occasional minor distortion

key_highlights: Pigpen’s Lovelight sequences drive the set with vivid organ texture
Bill Kreutzmann’s foot‑pedal solo and Mickey Hart’s cowbell create a rare, energetic drum duet
Jerry Garcia’s early lead work on Cumberland Blues shines with strong tone
Good soundboard capture preserves the high‑energy vibe despite minor vocal flutter
